step1_fiscal_year_pattern.pattern_classification: NEITHER contiguous NOR simple alternating NOR a single pre/post-date split. Non-zero years form three tight 2-year clusters -- {2012,2013}, {2017,2018}, {2024,2025} -- separated by multi-year zero-coverage gaps (2014-2016, 2019-2023) with a leading zero pair (2010-2011). Does NOT align cleanly with the era_definition_version regulatory boundaries in pm5_stage_table.csv (E1 2010-2012 is mixed zero/nonzero; E4 2016-2019 is mixed; E6 2023-2025 is mixed), so era membership does not explain the split. FY2011 (1 download) and FY2015 (2 downloads) are negligible trickle, not meaningfully different from the fully-zero years.

fetched_at_timestamp_clustering.finding: All 194 historical successful downloads have fetched_at timestamps within a single continuous ~4.5-minute window on 2026-09-11 (10:28:44 to 10:33:08 UTC). Within that one run, successes for each non-zero FY cluster arrive in tight, mutually-exclusive sub-windows in FY order: FY2012/2013 first (10:28:44-10:29:58), FY2017/2018 next (10:30:04-10:31:26), then FY2024/2025 last (10:31:29-10:33:08), with negligible trickle for FY2011 and FY2015 interleaved. This rules out 'separate partial crawl runs per research phase, run on different days' as the explanation -- it was one run -- and instead points to a time/session-dependent condition on the source side (e.g. exchange-side bot-mitigation state) as the more likely mechanism, which P-C0 can test directly against the committed code.

step3_raw_http_diagnostic.method: Two curl passes per URL from this session's live network (IIT Kanpur campus network, DNS via ns2.iitk.ac.in): (1) bare curl, default curl User-Agent, -L --max-time 30; (2) curl -L --max-time 45 --max-redirs 10 --retry 2 --retry-delay 3 (retries transient errors up to 3 total attempts). Full response headers, first 500 bytes of body, and curl's own stderr/exit code were captured verbatim for every attempt. No ARPipe code was invoked or modified for this step.

failure_modes_seen: CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT (28) - no response within 45s, repeated across all 3 retry attempts
summary.key_finding: Every sampled nsearchives.nseindia.com URL failed identically today regardless of whether it came from a ZERO-coverage FY (2010,2014,2015,2016) or a NONZERO-coverage FY (2012,2013,2017,2018,2024) -- 9 of 9 failed, with the same two failure modes (reset / timeout) distributed across both groups with no visible pattern tied to group membership. The single BSE URL tested (a ZERO-coverage company-year, Infosys FY2011) returned a clean HTTP 200 with a valid 5,698,015-byte PDF (magic bytes %PDF-1.6, Last-Modified: 2011-10-20, so the file has existed since shortly after the original filing and is not a recently-vanished source). Both nsearchives.nseindia.com and www.bseindia.com are Akamai-fronted, so generic 'no bot can reach Akamai' is not the explanation either; the block/reset is specific to the NSE archive host's configuration, not a general internet-reachability problem.

step4_committed_fetch_logic_comparison.how_fetch_one_evaluates_a_response: arpipe/fetch.py:fetch_one() streams GET with follow_redirects=True, timeout=120s, up to 3 attempts. 403/429/503 trigger a sleep-and-continue retry (quadratic backoff); any other exception (including connection reset and timeout, exactly what today's raw probes hit) is caught, logged to last_err, retried after a linear backoff, and after 3 attempts the original exception is re-raised. cmd_fetch's _fetch_pair() catches that re-raised exception, prints a one-line WARN to stderr (f'WARN fetch failover {company_id} {fy_end} [{source}]: {type(exc).__name__}'), and moves to the next candidate source in priority order (NSE -> BSE -> screener) for that company-year; if all candidates raise, the pair is simply absent from documents.jsonl with no structured reason recorded anywhere.
step4_committed_fetch_logic_comparison.why_this_explains_REASON_CODE_MISSING: reports/pm5_reason_code_completeness.csv (frozen P-M5 evidence, read-only) shows 0.0% reason-code coverage for BOTH the DISCOVERY and DOWNLOAD stages (0/64 and 0/318), versus 100% for IDENTITY and 90.7% for ACCEPTANCE. This is exactly consistent with fetch.py/cli.py's code path above: download failures are only ever printed to stderr (ephemeral console output that pm5_coverage.py's read-only reconciliation never captures), whereas verify.py/triage.py's later stages do write structured reason codes into live_dataset/manifest.jsonl. This is a code-verifiable, non-speculative finding, not an inference.
step4_committed_fetch_logic_comparison.asymmetry_identified_between_discovery_a: arpipe/discover.py:nse_session() builds an httpx.Client with NSE_HEADERS (Referer set to the NSE corporate-filings page) and first GETs www.nseindia.com twice to acquire cookies before calling the annual-reports API -- this is the client used ONLY for cmd_discover's discover_nse() calls, i.e. for finding the URLs. arpipe/cli.py:cmd_fetch() builds a completely separate, fresh httpx.Client (headers={'User-Agent': discover.UA} only, no Referer, no cookies from the discovery session) and this is the client fetch_one() uses to actually download the file from nsearchives.nseindia.com. Since nsearchives.nseindia.com is a distinct Akamai-fronted host from api/www.nseindia.com, whether it requires the discovery-stage session state (cookies and/or Referer) to avoid bot-mitigation resets is a concrete, testable, code-level hypothesis for why NSE archive downloads fail while a vanilla same-host browse might succeed -- and it is directly testable in P-C0 by replaying fetch_one with vs without the discovery session's cookie jar, without modifying any implementation.
step4_committed_fetch_logic_comparison.would_committed_head_accept_todays_obser: For the 9 NSE URLs: no. All 9 raised connection-level exceptions (reset/timeout) that do not fall into fetch_one's (403,429,503)-retry branch; they fall into the generic except-Exception branch, retry 3x with the exact same client/headers as our curl replica, and would raise after all 3 attempts -- i.e. running committed fetch_one() against these URLs today would almost certainly reproduce the same DOWNLOAD-stage failure with no captured reason, matching the frozen evidence's first_failed_stage=DOWNLOAD / first_failed_reason_code=REASON_CODE_MISSING rows exactly. For the 1 BSE URL: yes, fetch_one() would accept it (200, PDF, no retry needed) and store it -- this is a ZERO-coverage company-year (Infosys FY2011), so the fact that a live, fetchable, valid source exists for it today indicates the original DOWNLOAD-stage loss for this specific pair is not explained by a permanently vanished source.
step4_committed_fetch_logic_comparison.was_the_historical_run_necessarily_on_he: AMBIGUOUS, and explicitly flagged rather than assumed: reports/tools/pm5_coverage.py states in its own docstring that it 'does not import arpipe production modules and does not run discover / fetch / triage / segment / verify / extract' -- it only reconciles pre-existing log/snapshot files that were produced by some EARLIER real run of the CLI. That earlier run's discovery/download snapshot dates are 2026-09-11, and arpipe-0.1.0's tree is confirmed dirty right now with uncommitted changes to fetch.py, pipeline.py, cli.py and others -- so it cannot be proven from this evidence alone that the 2026-09-11 crawl ran against code byte-identical to HEAD 0fb8cbf. This does not block sufficiency (criterion 3 only requires that HEAD contain enough logic to compare against observed behavior, not proof of historical code identity), but P-C0 should treat 'was the crawl running HEAD-equivalent fetch.py' as an open sub-question worth checking (e.g. via git reflog / any run logs) rather than an assumption.

findings.url_pattern: IDENTICAL structure in both groups: nsearchives.nseindia.com/annual_reports/AR_<optional-numeric-id>_<SYMBOL>_<FY0>_<FY1>_<timestamp>.<zip|pdf>, matched by the same parse_nse_url_filename() regex in discover.py for both groups' samples.
findings.hostname: Same hostname (nsearchives.nseindia.com) for 9 of 10 samples across both groups; the 1 outlier (BSE) happens to fall in the ZERO group by sampling coincidence, not because BSE-vs-NSE tracks the zero/nonzero split.
findings.file_extension: Both groups are dominated by .zip (4/5 zero-group samples, 4/5 nonzero-group samples); the one .pdf sample (TataSteel FY2024) is in the NONZERO group, so extension does not separate the groups either.
findings.redirects: None observed in either group today (num_redirects=0 for all 10, both the successful BSE and the failing NSE attempts).
findings.status_codes_today: 9 NSE URLs (4 from the zero-group: FY2010/2014/2015/2016, and 5 from the nonzero-group: FY2012/2013/2017/2018/2024) -> no HTTP status at all (connection-level failure before a status line was received); 1 BSE URL (zero-group, FY2011) -> 200.
findings.auth_behavior: No authentication, cookies, or special headers were required for the one URL that succeeded (plain GET, default headers). No evidence either way for the 9 that failed at the connection level (never reached a point where auth could be evaluated).
findings.conclusion: STATE PLAINLY: no structural difference in URL, hostname, path, extension, or declared source was found between the zero-coverage and non-zero-coverage sampled company-years. The only measurable difference in the FROZEN evidence is the fetched_at timestamp clustering (Step 1), which is temporal, not structural. Today's live raw HTTP probing found NO group-based difference either -- both groups' NSE URLs failed identically. This rules out (with direct evidence, not assumption) a source-identifier or file-format explanation, and is consistent with a time/session/rate-limit-state-dependent mechanism on the NSE side that happened to align with which company-years were in flight during favorable windows of the original single 4.5-minute crawl run.
